Okay, here's the U.S. Core Inflation Rate (Year-over-Year) from January 2015 through December 2016, presented as a Markdown table. I'll use the Core CPI (Consumer Price Index excluding food and energy) data, which is a common measure.  The data below can be found, among other places, on the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) website.

| Month      | Year | Core Inflation Rate (YoY) |
|------------|------|---------------------------|
| January    | 2015 | 1.6%                      |
| February   | 2015 | 1.7%                      |
| March      | 2015 | 1.7%                      |
| April      | 2015 | 1.8%                      |
| May        | 2015 | 1.7%                      |
| June       | 2015 | 1.8%                      |
| July       | 2015 | 1.8%                      |
| August     | 2015 | 1.9%                      |
| September  | 2015 | 1.9%                      |
| October    | 2015 | 2.0%                      |
| November   | 2015 | 2.0%                      |
| December   | 2015 | 2.1%                      |
| January    | 2016 | 2.2%                      |
| February   | 2016 | 2.3%                      |
| March      | 2016 | 2.2%                      |
| April      | 2016 | 2.1%                      |
| May        | 2016 | 2.2%                      |
| June       | 2016 | 2.2%                      |
| July       | 2016 | 2.2%                      |
| August     | 2016 | 2.3%                      |
| September  | 2016 | 2.2%                      |
| October    | 2016 | 2.2%                      |
| November   | 2016 | 2.1%                      |
| December   | 2016 | 2.2%                      |

**Important Notes:**

*   **Source:** This data is based on the Core CPI (Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers; All Items Less Food and Energy) published by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).  You can find the official data and methodology on the BLS website (www.bls.gov).
*   **Year-over-Year (YoY):** The percentage change represents the inflation rate compared to the same month in the *previous* year.
*   **Core CPI:**  Core CPI is often watched more closely than the headline CPI because it's considered a better indicator of underlying inflation trends by excluding volatile food and energy prices.
